item.title: Pitch for defense treaty and moving US military to Israel is insane
item.description:
On August 18, Israel bombed a non-operational Syrian air base, reportedly to derail Turkish plans to deploy military forces to the installation. The move drew swift condemnation from the United States, which did not receive prior notification despite its growing support for Syria, its alliance with Turkey, and the presence of thousands of U.S. military personnel based nearby, in Jordan and other parts of the region.

Is this the behavior of a “model ally”? The Jewish Institute for National Security of America seems to think so.

The group, which promotes "strategic cooperation" between the United States and Israel, tries to defend this position in its new report, “Shifting the Center of Gravity: Transforming the U.S.-Israel Security Partnership.” It also lays out an ambitious set of proposals JINSA hopes will be part of a renewed 10-year U.S.-Israel Memorandum of Understanding (the current one expires in 2028). JINSA wants this "final" direct aid package to include $38 billion total and be "paired with new, mostly non-monetary initiatives that deepen and expand the U.S.-Israel partnership."

The recommendations in this report — which also include signing a mutual defense pact, basing U.S. military forces in Israel, and integrating Israeli technology into U.S. homeland defense — should be rejected as threats to U.S. national security. Not only would they cost taxpayers tens of billions of dollars, but the prescriptions would make the United States less safe than it is today, by institutionalizing U.S. military entanglement with (and even dependence on) Israel and increasing the risk of future wars.

Instead the Trump administration should instead let the current MoU expire in 2028 with no replacement. With a strong military and nuclear arsenal, Israel can defend itself.

The JINSA report opens by heralding Israel as “America’s most important ally,” praising its military prowess, technological capability, and willingness to project military power in pursuit of supposedly shared goals. Missing from its account of Israel’s support during Operation Epic Fury, however, is any mention of Israel’s role in starting, escalating, or widening the war. These are certainly relevant details if we are judging whether the bilateral relationship is an asset or a liability to the United States.

The report sidesteps these realities and instead moves quickly to a set of 10 proposals that it argues will take the bilateral partnership to the “next level.” From the perspective of protecting U.S. national interests, these ideas range from bad to insane.

Among the more worrying recommendations are those that suggest the United States should form a mutual defense treaty with Israel and begin shifting U.S. assets away from current positions in the Persian Gulf to a wider and permanent force posture in Israel — including a new CENTCOM headquarters and a "regional U.S. prepositioned arsenal hub." These would break long-established firewalls in the U.S.-Israel relationship and undermine U.S. interests.

Since 1975, the United States has had a security commitment to Israel, formalized in a memorandum of agreement, that promises “remedial action” should Israel face external threat. In recent years, this commitment has functioned as a de facto security guarantee on par with Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. Still, the United States has intentionally refrained from signing a more explicit mutual defense agreement with Israel or basing U.S. personnel inside Israel’s borders for two reasons.

First, it was Israel’s preference. Jerusalem has long prided itself on the fact that only its soldiers directly defend the country and that it could fight its own battles as long as the United States offered military support. Second, Washington feared a more formal defense obligation or forward bases in Israel would increase the risk that the United States would eventually become entangled in Israel’s ongoing border skirmishes or complicate relationships with U.S. Gulf state partners, like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, on whom the United States relied to keep oil prices low.

The recommendations by JINSA, which count 43 retired U.S. officers — including 24 generals and nine admirals — on its roster, discard these redlines. The mutual defense agreement they describe is framed as a narrow one that would be triggered “by the high bar of existential threat to Israel or Iranian use of weapons of mass destruction against U.S. bases in the region.” But history tells us that, for Israel, the “existential threat” threshold is met easily and often.

In recent years, Israel has argued that Iran posed an existential threat while also claiming Hezbollah and Hamas as existential challenges to Israel’s security. In other words, signing onto this agreement would all but guarantee U.S. involvement in future Middle East wars against Iran or possibly even Turkey, which some in Israel have already identified as the next target despite the fact that it is a NATO ally.

Of course, this is the goal of the recommendation: to ensure that no matter how far Israel falls in U.S. public opinion, the United States will be obligated to come to its defense, or risk undermining the credibility of its other commitments.

Basing U.S military forces inside Israel would only worsen the moral hazard engendered by U.S. support to the country. With U.S. personnel as a tripwire, Israel’s leaders would feel assured that any attack would almost certainly drag in the United States, giving them little incentive to act with restraint. The risk that the United States might be ensnared in Israel’s future military adventures would be high.

The second major focus of JINSA’s recommendations covers the sharing of military technology and joint industrial projects between Israel and the United States. Most of these proposals demand that Israel gain the same level of access to U.S. technology as is enjoyed by the closest NATO allies who have spent years working to meet U.S. security standards. That Israeli officials are suspected of spying on the United States should be warning enough that giving Israel this type of access to sensitive U.S. technology would be a mistake.

The most dangerous of these tech sharing ideas, however, is one suggesting that Israeli technologies should be directly integrated into U.S. air and missile defense, specifically the Golden Dome project. This provision would mean that, if the Golden Dome project or something like it eventually covers the United States, Israeli technology would be part of its foundation, making the U.S. dependent on Israel for its own defense.

The United States tried something similar once before with Israel and the project had to be cancelled. The reason? Israel refused to allow the United States access to the source code needed to integrate the Iron Dome systems it planned to purchase into the U.S. air defense network. Experimenting with this type of cooperation a second time would be an act of self-harm on the part of the U.S. government.

Taken together, then, the JINSA proposals do not advance U.S. interests in the Middle East or elsewhere. In fact, they do just the opposite. They will increase the U.S. security burden and tie the United States down in the Middle East in ways that may quickly become irreversible while also undermining the physical security of the homeland. And they will do so at a cost of $38 billion from U.S. taxpayers in the form of annual military aid.

This outcome should be entirely unacceptable to any American president, regardless of the specific ally or partner in question and especially for a president who ran on promises to put U.S. interests first.

Elsewhere, President Donald Trump is pushing allies to defend themselves without so much (or any) U.S. support. He should do the same with Israel. The endless cycle of MoUs has run its course. The current one should be the last.

item.title: Trump can huff & puff but without political fix Iran won't come down
item.description:
The latest U.S. strategy in the Middle East is defined as one of “maximum pressure,” combining military containment and economic sanctions in an attempt to compel Iran to accept a deal. But it lacks clearly defined, civilian-led outcomes, illustrating the persistent misalignment between military means and political ends.

Military pressure can set conditions, signal resolve, and buy time for civilian action. It cannot determine political outcomes. When a civilian-led strategy rooted in clear end states is not determined ahead of sending military forces, those deployments turn into continuous rotations; it is how ‘forever wars’ get started.

This essay is not an argument against the use of force. It is at times necessary, and even realist restraint doctrine says so. Instead, this essay is an argument that force is but one of many instruments of national security; when the other instruments of national security, like diplomacy, aren’t employed equally or greater than the military, it is service members who pay the greatest price.

An earlier article laid the framework for this argument; this article shows what the habit of overreliance on the military looks like in practice. It is about what happens when whole-of-government strategic planning doesn’t take place before the first bullet is fired – leading to strategic failure even if the military objective is achieved.

On March 4, 2026, U.S. Army Vice Chief of Staff General LaNeve testified that more than 108,000 U.S. Army soldiers only (not counting military forces from the other services) were deployed or forwardly postured across 160 countries. Many, more than 50,000 personnel from all the services, are deployed to the U.S. Central Command area of interest in the Middle East. They include sailors still at sea aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln. These forces have frequently been deployed to display U.S. resolve or apply “pressure” but have remained overseas longer than they or others anticipated.

Legendary deterrence theorist Thomas Schelling described a difference between using force to physically destroy an adversary's capability and using force as a threat to change an adversary's behavior. The former is a military task; the latter is a political strategy, effective only if a settlement is feasible. According to Schelling, "the power to hurt is bargaining power." But when pressure is applied without the possibility of a political settlement, force is all that remains.

In the 1991 Gulf War, the U.S. military stopped after liberating Kuwait and declined to advance to Baghdad. The political and military leadership (of President George H.W. Bush and Gens. Colin Powell and Norman Schwarzkopf, Jr.) agreed that continuing to Baghdad would trade a decisive military victory for an open-ended occupation for which the country wasn’t prepared. That was a wise political decision made before forces were committed.

Twelve years later, the U.S. political leadership ordered an invasion of Iraq without first answering the question of who would pick up the pieces after the military had done its job. While postwar civilian authorities were established, they were deployed too late, and post-conflict planning failed to assign civilian responsibilities and resources for security beyond military control. What was missing was the whole-of-government strategy on the who, what, where, when, and how the desired political outcome was to be achieved.

"You are going to be the proud owner of 25 million people,” then-Secretary of State Powell warned President George W. Bush before the invasion. “You will own all their hopes, aspirations, and problems. You'll own it all.” His warning, later dubbed the Pottery Barn rule — “if you break it, you own it” — underlined the importance of allocating responsibility for planning for the “day after” the use of force. The answer must always be America’s elected civilian leadership, not the uniformed members of the military; answers to the “who, what, where” questions must be known before forces are committed, not afterwards.

In Afghanistan, the military removed the regime and won on the battlefield. But multiple U.S. administrations failed to answer what specific, achievable, and time-bound political outcomes the fighting was designed to achieve. Instead, drawdown plans were based on optimistic assumptions and insufficient preparation for a full withdrawal. So when the political decision was finally made to bring the troops home and abandon Kabul in 2021, it was done in a hurried and improvisational manner, turning the operation into an evacuation, on the fly and under fire.

The 2026 Iran war has followed a similar pattern. On February 28, U.S. and Israeli aircraft struck Iran, opening the current phase of the conflict. While the military achieved its tactical objectives, there was no clearly defined civilian-led strategy to achieve the publicly stated political goal of overthrowing the Iranian regime, or at least forcing it to make significant concessions. An interim agreement established a 60-day negotiating period for a final agreement and temporarily paused military operations, but, without a clear political strategy, this had little hope of succeeding.

The result has been a return to violence as both sides claim to control, or even own, the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. forces are once again deployed to the Middle East with no end in sight. What started as a military pressure campaign to first destroy nuclear-related infrastructure and then remove the regime — something pressure alone (particularly air pressure only) can never achieve — has turned into the longest ever deployment of a U.S. aircraft carrier at sea without a port call and another “forever” conflict.

Ordering the deployment of forces is easy, but disengagement and redeployment are hard work. Powell used eight questions, and former Defense Secretary Casper Weinberger set down six criteria, including requirements that combat be a last resort and objectives be clearly defined before commitment. Which model used doesn’t matter so much as adhering to a model. It’s the discipline to not get into a fight without an exit strategy.

This touches on one reason the military is repeatedly asked to accomplish strategic outcomes beyond its mandate. Unlike other government institutions, the military teaches strategy and planning, and at scale. It has dedicated masters degree-granting institutions and dedicated career fields, such as the U.S. Army’s Functional Area 59 (Strategist). In contrast, the Department of State has genuine expertise, and its foreign service officers execute complex diplomatic missions every day, but it lacks a year-long, in-residence, career-gated strategist program; so does every other major agency that make up the other elements of national security.

The fix is for the president and Congress to build civilian capacity, tied to career advancement, to the same degrees the military currently possesses. Then, when national leadership convenes the government’s national security experts to consider the use of force, it is the civilian strategist who must be heard in at least equal measure as the military planner.

Unfortunately, when the government equates military pressure to strategy, it asks military forces to do the work that would be far more appropriately assigned to their political, diplomatic, or development counterparts. Military forces are designed to close with and destroy the enemy, not negotiate or oversee political settlements.

Deploying teams into high-risk environments and getting them home safely is common operational preparation. Every unit that deploys does it. Every combatant command does it. What is missing is the same preparation at the level above the uniform, from the civilian political leadership appointed over the military. Before you send them, know how, and when, you bring them back. Anything less is not strategy. It is the beginning of another long deployment.

item.title: Israel's Netanyahu says Iran tried to kill one of his sons
item.description:
TEL AVIV, Aug 24 (Reuters) - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday that Iran had tried to kill one of his sons, but gave no details about when the alleged plot took place, which son was targeted or how close it came to being carried out.

Netanyahu's allegation underscores the heightened tensions since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began in February, during which Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior Iranian leaders were killed.

item.title: US removes Syria from terrorism sponsor list, lifting major investment obstacle
item.description:
By Feras Dalatey

DAMASCUS, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The United States removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism on Monday, lifting what Damascus says was the last major impediment to investing in the country as Washington deepens ties to the new Syrian government.

The removal, posted on the U.S. Treasury's website, took effect after a 45-day congressional review period triggered when Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the designation.

item.title: Saudi Arabia to invest $7 bn in theme parks near Paris: French presidency
item.description:
France and Saudi Arabia on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding for a six-billion-euro ($7 billion) Saudi investment to create three theme parks near Paris, including one likely to be manga-themed, the office of the French president said.

The French presidency's Elysee Palace said the agreement for the "colossal" project was signed during a two-day visit to France by Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

item.title: US removes Syria's designation as State Sponsor of Terrorism list
item.description:
Aug 24 (Reuters) - The State Department on Monday removed Syria from its list of State Sponsors of Terrorism, according to a notification from the U.S. Treasury, in a move that was first announced earlier this year pending a review by Congress.

The designation as a state sponsor of terrorism carries restrictions on U.S. foreign assistance, defense exports and certain financial transactions.

Monday's announcement also removed the designation of the Nusrah Front as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization.

item.title: US removes Syria from state sponsor of terrorism list
item.description:
The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, rescinding a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions and marking another step in warming ties between the countries.

The US Department of State also revoked its designation of al-Nusra Front -- latterly known as Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) -- as a global terrorist organization. The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief.

item.title: Oil prices fall as Bessent outlines new steps to punish Iran
item.description:
Oil prices retreated as US Treasury Secretary outlined plans for more sanctions to punish Iran while stock markets mostly faltered on Monday as investors looked ahead to key US inflation data and earnings from Nvidia.

While late August is typically a slow news period for markets, the US-Iran war, a trade battle between the United States and Canada and results from artificial intelligence bellwether Nvidia are keeping markets engaged.
